title: First report of PLS
abstract: The emergence and dissemination of antimicrobial resistance through the food chain pose a significant threat to food safety and public health. Our nationwide surveillance of retail foods in China revealed alarmingly high resistance rates among foodborne Staphylococcus isolates, particularly to antibiotics targeting the 50S ribosomal subunit. Among these, Mammaliicoccus lentus (formerly Staphylococcus lentus) is a coagulase-negative species commonly found in food-producing animals and retail foods, increasingly recognized as a reservoir of antimicrobial resistance genes. To elucidate the genetic basis of this severe phenotype, we identified M. lentus strain M177 from retail potato flour exhibiting exceptionally high resistance to tiamulin, clindamycin, and lincomycin, a profile unexplained by known resistance genes. Targeted BLASTp analysis identified a putative ARE ABC-F gene sharing 98.71% amino acid identity with Sal(B), which we designated sal(B). Functional validation confirmed that Sal(B) confers specific resistance to PLS

title: Expression profiling of the gibberellin 2-oxidase gene CsGA2ox2 (Cucumis sativus L.) reveals stage- and tissue-specific transcript accumulation during fruit development.
abstract: Gibberellins (GAs) regulate fruit set and expansion, and their endogenous levels are controlled in part through catabolic inactivation. GA2ox enzymes convert bioactive GAs into inactive forms, but the expression of GA2ox genes during cucumber fruit development has not been characterised in a tissue-resolved manner. Cucumber (Cucumis sativus L.) '9930' fruit were sampled at 0, 7, 14, 21 and 28 days after pollination. The inner fleshy tissue (pulp) and the outer fruit wall (pericarp) were separated, and CsGA2ox2 transcript abundance was quantified by quantitative real-time PCR using the 2^ CsGA2ox2 was transcribed at every developmental stage examined. Transcript abundance was low at 0 and 7 days after pollination, increased significantly by 21 days after pollination, and was consistently and significantly higher in pulp than in pericarp at all stages examined. The gene encodes a 342-residue protein sharing 71.84%-74.96% amino acid identity with GA2ox homologues of other cucurbits. It is predicted to be an unstable, hydrophilic, non-secretory protein whose secondary structure is dominated by random coils, and its promoter contains abscisic acid-, light- and meristem-responsive cis-acting elements. CsGA2ox2 shows stage- and tissue-specific transcript accumulation during cucumber fruit development, with a marked bias toward the pulp. All protein-level results presented here are computational predictions and provide no direct functional evidence. The data are descriptive and correlative and are intended as a foundation for future functional studies on GA catabolism in Cucurbitaceae fruit development.

title: The wisdom of the diverse crowd(funders)
abstract: Crowdfunding platforms aim to democratize entrepreneurial finance by creating ecosystems that elicit the ‘wisdom of crowds’—aggregating the judgments of individual and often amateur funders. However, there is limited evidence on whether crowds can effectively apply their collective wisdom on these platforms. Our study addresses these questions by analyzing a crowdlending platform that connects Western lenders with borrowers in developing countries. We examine whether lenders effectively screen borrowers, identify platform attributes that influence lenders’ screening accuracy, and uncover the underlying mechanisms driving these effects. To achieve this, we exploit interventions by platform administrators that allow us to observe the counterfactual repayment performance of loans that failed to attract sufficient funding. Our results indicate that rowdlenders can effectively screen creditworthy borrowers, but only when financial information about borrowers is made available. Lenders’ screening effectiveness diminishes substantially for prosocial loans, as many funders converge on similar, socially motivated decisions. These findings provide novel evidence on crowdlenders' performance, highlighting key trade-offs for crowdfunding platforms and offering actionable insights for their administrators.

title: DETERMINING FACTORS OF INTENTION TO PAY ZAKAT VIA FINANCIAL TECHNOLOGY (FINTECH)
abstract: This study aims to examine muzakki’s intention to utilize Financial Technology (Fintech) platforms for paying zakat by investigating the behavioral and psychological determinants. The research integrates the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB), with a particular emphasis on prosocial motivations and perceived risk factors. This study uniquely expanded the view of perceived risk variables, including psychological, legal, and time risks, by integrating altruism and empathy as prosocial constructs into a single framework. The research employs a quantitative approach, utilizing a structured questionnaire distributed to 150 purposively selected respondents. The data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares-Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) to test the relationships between the variables. The findings reveal that perceived altruism and empathy significantly influence muzakki’s intention to adopt fintech for zakat contributions. In contrast, perceived risk—which encompasses aspects such as privacy, legality, time, psychological burden, and security—does not have a significant effect on the intention to use fintech for zakat. These results suggest that emotional and social motivations are stronger predictors of digital zakat payment adoption than perceived risk. Therefore, zakat institutions and fintech developers are advised to focus on building trust and emphasizing the altruistic and empathetic values of zakat in their platforms, as this effort is expected to strengthen the development of a sharia-compliant digital financial ecosystem and contribute to achieving social goals, such as poverty alleviation and reducing inequality.

title: The Life-sustenance Hypothesis: Understanding Human-Nature Connection by Integrating Rousseau's Philosophy to Contemporary Systems Biological Viewpoints
abstract: This paper develops the life-sustenance hypothesis to explain the multifaceted phenomenon of the human-nature connection. It is based on an interpretation of Jean-Jacques Rousseau’s philosophy brought into contemporary times via recent multidisciplinary research and theoretical underpinnings. Rousseau suggested that humans have two innate, instinctive drives he called amour-de-soi and pitié—a self-preservative drive, and its enlargement, an inclination to help other living beings in distress. The life-sustenance hypothesis is rooted in a systems biological framework situating humans as interconnected parts within a nested system of life. Corresponding to Rousseau’s drives, this interconnectedness is suggested to give rise to the dynamics between two life-preserving orientations that guide our manners-of-being in the world: a self-sustaining and a ‘life-sustaining’ orientation shared by all organisms, albeit manifested differently. The experience of nature connectedness, along with altruistic impulses, are proposed to be human manifestations of the life-sustaining orientation. Moreover, in line with Rousseau’s philosophy, it is posited that the modern, individualistic lifestyle has given rise to an imbalance between these orientations leading to problems in prosociality, proenvironmentalism, and overall well-being. One means by which to regain balanced manners-of-being might be to enhance our nature connectedness. Possible physiological indicators for the hypothesis are explored.

title: Perceptions and Experiences of the Foster Family Program Among Alumni and Undergraduate Medical Students at CMC Ludhiana: An Exploratory Mixed-Methods Study.
abstract: Mentorship plays a crucial role in the holistic development of medical students. The Foster Family Program (FFP) at Christian Medical College (CMC), Ludhiana, is a unique mentorship model that provides academic, emotional, social, and spiritual support through a family-like structure involving faculty mentors ("foster parents") and students ("foster siblings"). To describe and explore foster parents' and foster siblings' retrospective perceptions of the FFP, including reported support, engagement, relationship continuity, strengths, challenges, and suggestions for improvement. A mixed-methods study was conducted among MBBS alumni of CMC Ludhiana (batches 1960-2015), including foster parents and foster siblings. Quantitative data were collected via a structured online questionnaire using snowball sampling and analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics. Qualitative data were obtained through open-ended responses and analyzed using thematic analysis. Key domains assessed included academic performance, mental health, interpersonal relationships, and career development. A total of 227 participants were included, comprising 24 (10.6%) foster parents and 203 (89.4%) foster siblings. The mean age of foster parents was 49.6 years, and that of foster siblings was 21.2 years. Most participants reported positive outcomes, with 15 (65.2%) rating the program highly. Interpersonal relationships were strengthened in 20 (87.0%) of the foster parents, while 14 (60.9%) discussed mental health concerns with their fosters. 120 (61.2%) students reported receiving support during stressful periods, and 109 (55.3%) identified their mentor as inspirational. Long-term relationships persisted, with 17 (77.3%) between foster parents and students, while 13 (6.6%) kept in touch with their foster parents only and 91 (46%) with both foster parents and siblings maintaining contact after graduation. Qualitative analysis revealed key strengths, including emotional support, academic and spiritual guidance, a safe space for sharing, and community bonding. Reported challenges included inactivity of some foster families, time constraints, financial burden, mismatched expectations, and interpersonal discomfort. The FFP was associated with perceived improvements in the academic, psychosocial, and emotional well-being of medical students. While overall perceptions were positive, variability in engagement highlights the need for improved mentor-mentee matching and more structured interaction. The model demonstrates potential for replication, although contextual adaptation may be necessary.

title: The effect of psilocybin on empathy and prosocial behavior: a proposed mechanism for enduring antidepressant effects
abstract: Psilocybin is a serotonergic psychedelic shown to have enduring antidepressant effects. Currently, the mechanism for its enduring effects is not well understood. Empathy and prosocial behavior may be important for understanding the therapeutic benefit of psilocybin. In this article we review the effect of psilocybin on empathy and prosocial behavior. Moreover, we propose that psilocybin may induce a positive feedback loop involving empathy and prosocial behavior which helps explain the observed, enduring antidepressant effects.

title: Drivers of cooperation in social dilemmas on higher‐order networks
abstract: Understanding cooperation in social dilemmas requires models that capture the complexity of real-world interactions. While network frameworks have provided valuable insights to model the evolution of cooperation, they are unable to encode group interactions properly. Here, we introduce a general higher-order networks framework for multi-player games on structured populations. Our model considers multi-dimensional strategies, based on the observation that social behaviours are affected by the size of the group interaction. We investigate the dynamical and structural coupling between different orders of interactions, revealing the crucial role of nested multi-level interactions and showing how such features can enhance cooperation beyond the limit of traditional models with uni-dimensional strategies. Our work identifies the key drivers promoting cooperative behaviour commonly observed in real-world group social dilemmas.

title: How do neurorehabilitation patients perceive their fundamental care needs? Findings from a qualitative study.
abstract: The Fundamentals of Care (FoC) framework provides a structured model to support the delivery of person-centered nursing care by integrating physical, psychosocial, and relational dimensions. Although the framework has been widely applied in acute care, little is known about its relevance in long-term neurorehabilitation settings, where patients often face complex, prolonged, and multidimensional care needs. To explore how individuals with neurological disorders perceive their fundamental care needs during inpatient rehabilitation. A qualitative secondary analysis. A rehabilitation hospital in Italy with a total capacity of 109 beds. We recruited individuals aged 18 years and older with a diagnosis of stroke, multiple sclerosis, or Parkinson disease, or who had undergone neurosurgical intervention for oncological conditions. A deductive content analysis was performed, using the FoC framework to guide coding and thematic development. The analysis identified care experiences across the three FoC dimensions. In the physical dimension, patients valued hygiene, toileting, mobility, and comfort not only as technical tasks but also as meaningful acts that contributed to dignity and recovery. The psychosocial dimension emphasized the importance of respectful communication, emotional support, privacy, and being informed, factors that fostered agency and trust. In the relational dimension, patients highlighted empathy, continuity, and presence as central to feeling emotionally safe and supported. Health care assistants emerged as key figures in delivering comfort-focused and relational care. Across all dimensions, fundamental care was perceived as deeply interconnected and resistant to rigid, task-based models. This study underscores the value of the FoC framework in capturing the multidimensional nature of care as experienced by neurorehabilitation patients. The findings reinforce the need for nurses and assistants to provide care that extends beyond physical tasks to include relational presence and person-centered responsiveness.

title: Resolving social dilemmas with minimal reward transfer
abstract: Abstract Social dilemmas present a significant challenge in multi-agent cooperation because individuals are incentivised to behave in ways that undermine socially optimal outcomes. Consequently, self-interested agents often avoid collective behaviour. In response, we formalise social dilemmas and introduce a novel metric, the general self-interest level, to quantify the disparity between individual and group rationality in such scenarios. This metric represents the maximum proportion of their individual rewards that agents can retain while ensuring that a social welfare optimum becomes a dominant strategy. Our approach diverges from traditional concepts of altruism, instead focusing on strategic reward redistribution. By transferring rewards among agents in a manner that aligns individual and group incentives, rational agents will maximise collective welfare while pursuing their own interests. We provide an algorithm to compute efficient transfer structures for an arbitrary number of agents, and introduce novel multi-player social dilemma games to illustrate the effectiveness of our method. This work provides both a descriptive tool for analysing social dilemmas and a prescriptive solution for resolving them via efficient reward transfer contracts. Applications include mechanism design, where we can assess the impact on collaborative behaviour of modifications to models of environments.

title: Co-designing engagement principles for involving children and young people in palliative care research in low- and middle-income settings.
abstract: Engaging children in research processes is recognised as best practice, as it ensures studies are relevant and responsive to their needs. Limited evidence exists on effective approaches for engaging children with serious illnesses, particularly in palliative care and in resource-limited settings. This study aimed to work with children and young people with serious physical illness to co-design processes and practices for meaningful engagement and involvement in palliative care research within resource-limited settings. This qualitative, participatory study used three co-design workshops to develop engagement principles and practical processes for meaningfully involving children and young people in research. Twenty participants living with serious illnesses were purposively recruited from three heterogeneous tertiary care services in Uganda. Guided by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) principles for public involvement, workshops were facilitated by members of a multidisciplinary team, parents and caregivers. Workshop discussions, activity outputs and facilitator notes were analysed using framework analysis, with the NIHR principles as the initial framework, and the emerging principles were refined and agreed through consensus with participants. The resulting engagement principles are being implemented and evaluated within the parent research programme through an ongoing Child Advisory Group, enabling refinement of the engagement approach through iterative feedback from children, young people and researchers. The workshops therefore represent the initial phase of a broader programme, with Child Advisory Group activities planned through 2027. Nine principles for engaging and involving children and young people in palliative care research were co-designed. Examples include: Involve children early to ensure that objectives, questions and outputs are relevant to their needs and concerns; Creative and flexible co-design of workshop and meeting agendas makes sessions enjoyable, thus increasing attendance; Involvement of children in the design of research study materials ensures that they are child-centred and easily understood; Sharing decision-making power with children strengthens efficiency, coordination, communication, and group management. Early implementation through the Child Advisory Group indicated that the principles were feasible and acceptable to children, young people and researchers. Co-designed engagement principles can support meaningful involvement of children and young people throughout paediatric palliative care research. These findings provide practical guidance for establishing child-centred engagement approaches in resource-limited settings and may inform future research, policy and practice. Ongoing application of the principles by the Child Advisory Group through 2027 will allow their continued evaluation and refinement.

title: Basic Psychological Needs and Sustained Participation in Men's Sheds: Implications for Well-Being and Suicide Prevention.
abstract: Older men who endorse traditional masculine values such as stoicism and independence may be less likely to seek help when distressed, increasing vulnerability to social isolation and suicide. Men's Sheds, operating in 12 countries with around 3,000 sheds, offer practical activities, shared purpose, and informal social connection in settings that align with familiar masculine norms while providing support. Despite these benefits, many sheds struggle to maintain member engagement, and little is known about why some men remain involved over the long term while others disengage. This qualitative study, informed by self-determination theory (SDT), explored the processes associated with sustained participation. Twelve retired men aged 65-86 from three Men's Sheds participated in semi-structured interviews. Participants were primarily Anglo-Australian, with memberships ranging from 18 months to 25 years. Reflexive thematic analysis identified six themes: tentative beginnings, membership commitment, friendship and belonging, peer support, learning and mastery, and freedom of choice. Participants often joined following life transitions that had disrupted established sources of connection, purpose, capability, and routine. Continued participation was associated with opportunities for social connection and belonging, skill development and sharing, contributing to others, and exercising meaningful choice. These experiences closely corresponded to the SDT needs for relatedness, competence, and autonomy. The findings suggest that men's sheds may sustain long-term engagement by providing an environment that supports the satisfaction of basic psychological needs and promotes a renewed sense of purpose and well-being among older men.

title: Experts' Needs Assessment and Evaluation of Mobile Apps for Children of Parents With Mental Illness: Mixed Methods Study.
abstract: Children of parents with mental health illness (COPMI) have the right to receive preventive interventions to avoid developing their own mental health and socioeconomic problems. However, access to interventions varies widely within health care and social services depending on their geographical location in Sweden. In this regard, mobile health (mHealth) interventions for COPMI provide a pathway for more equitable and sustainable preventive support. This project aims to (1) map and assess the quality of available mHealth apps relevant to COPMI; (2) investigate experts' perceptions of COPMI needs for digital health solutions (particularly mHealth) by consulting and collaborating with an interdisciplinary reference group (scholars, child rights organizations, and IT professionals); and (3) explore the prerequisites for development, implementation, and sustainable access to future digital solutions for COPMI. We collaborated with a reference group through a series of meetings and workshops, identifying and assessing the quality of 9 free, highly ranked apps (ie, using the well-known Mobile App Rating Scale [MARS]). All the workshop sessions were recorded and transcribed for further qualitative analysis, allowing us to document and derive our main findings. Three out of 9 apps received high scores across the MARS dimensions of aesthetics, perceived functionality, information, and engagement in the expert heuristic evaluation using recorded demonstrations of the apps, indicating a significant lack of high-quality apps relevant to COPMI. Further findings were derived, such as the experts' preference for more general apps that are not specifically targeted to COPMI, as these could promote self-identification and reduce stigmatization. Regarding the third aim, the results showed that it was important to find an app that protected users' privacy by allowing anonymous access to digital support and that mobile apps should be complemented (or replaced) by web-based applications to improve accessibility for children who may not be allowed to download apps without parental permission. The sustainability of digital solutions (web applications or mobile apps) for COPMI is the biggest challenge for future developments. Long-term impact requires stable funding, continuous maintenance, and partnering with established organizations that already possess the infrastructure, expertise, and reach necessary to provide ongoing support. To address the limitations in the study design and deployment issues, it is important to actively involve children through participatory and co-creational approaches when designing and developing mHealth solutions. Also, future evaluations should include privacy and data security assessments such as app permissions, privacy-policy presence, and third-party sharing.

title: Is leisure‐time reading related to empathy and social skills in 8‐ to 10‐year‐old children?
abstract: There is growing interest in the effects of reading on empathy and prosocial behaviour but not enough is known about the associations among these variables in children. In a study undertaken at a single time point, we examined children's leisure reading and self-reported prosocial behaviour, and whether the relation between them was mediated by affective or cognitive empathy or by theory of mind. We tested 113 English-speaking children aged 8-10 years from a UK primary school. Analyses showed that reading and prosocial behaviour are related, and that the relation was partly explained by variance shared with empathy, particularly affective rather than cognitive empathy. Future work focusing on causal aspects of these relations should provide further guidance on the practical implications of these results.

title: Regional Consortia of Cancer Center Shared Resources: Models for Collaborative Infrastructure and the Emergence of a National Alliance.
abstract: Shared resource facilities are foundational to the scientific productivity of National Cancer Institute (NCI)-designated cancer centers, yet institutional silos frequently constrain member access to specialized instrumentation and expertise. Interinstitutional consortia of shared resources offer a pragmatic solution, enabling reciprocal service access at internal rates while preserving institutional autonomy. Here we describe two established regional consortia, the Mid-Atlantic Cancer Center Shared Resource Consortium (MACCSRC) and the Fred Hutchinson/University of Washington/Seattle Children's NCI Comprehensive Cancer Center Consortium-examining their organizational frameworks, operational outcomes, and lessons learned. Finally, we introduce the recently organized National Alliance for Cancer Center Shared Resources and discuss how it may serve as an integrating infrastructure connecting regional networks on a national scale. Key considerations for consortium formation, including governance, intellectual property, pricing harmonization, and cost allocation, are addressed.

title: MOOD AND EMPATHY ON PROSOCIAL BEHAVIOUR AMONG MUSLIM ADOLESCENTS IN PADANG CITY
abstract: This research is motivated by the phenomenon at the Dharmabakti Nusantara Health Vocational School in Padang City; mood and empathy are thought to influence prosocial behaviour. This study aims to analyse: 1) mood, empathy and prosocial behaviour, 2) the relationship between mood and prosocial behaviour, 3) the relationship between empathy and prosocial behaviour, and 4) the relationship between mood and empathy together with prosocial behaviour. The method used in this study is a Quantitative method that aims to determine the relationship and influence between variables. The research sample was taken from the existing population of 80 students. The research instrument used a questionnaire with a Likert scale model. The data were analysed with descriptive statistics, simple regression, and multiple regression; the results of the research data analysis obtained an R-value of 0.558 with a p level = 0.000 (p <0.05). There is a significant relationship between mood and empathy with prosocial behaviour. R2 =0,311 %. This study proves a positive and meaningful relationship between philosophy and heart in prosocial behaviour at SMK Dharmabakti Nusantara Pota Padang.

title: The Relationship between Well-Being, Empathy, Moral Identity, and Spirituality on Prosocial Behavior among Malaysian Youth
abstract: This study explores the influence of well-being, empathy, moral identity, and spirituality on prosocial behavior among Malaysian youth.A quantitative approach was employed with a sample of 411 participants, using Pearson correlation and multiple regression analyses to investigate the relationships between these variables.The results revealed that moral identity was the strongest predictor of prosocial behavior, followed closely by spirituality, empathy, and well-being.These findings highlight the central role of moral identity in shaping prosocial actions, with spirituality and empathy also playing significant roles.Well-being, while slightly less influential, still contributes meaningfully to prosocial behavior by promoting emotional stability and life satisfaction.The study emphasizes the importance of fostering moral development, spiritual growth, and emotional well-being to encourage prosocial behavior in youth.Policymakers, educators, and community leaders are encouraged to implement programs that focus on these key areas to promote a more compassionate and engaged youth population.

title: An exploration of the application and understanding of compassion from the perspective of parents and mental health nursing students
abstract: This thesis explores the application and understanding of compassion. Chapter one examines the application of compassion through Compassion-based Interventions (CBIs) for parents. Chapter two investigates the understanding of compassion from the perspective of Mental Health Nursing Students (MHNSs). Chapter one is a systematic literature review investigating CBIs for parents. The aims were to evaluate the effectiveness of CBIs on psychological factors, examine qualitative themes and integrate quantitative and qualitative knowledge. Ten moderate to high quality studies published between 2018 and 2020 were evaluated using a mixed studies design (Pluye & Hong, 2014). Samples were small and biased, limiting the strength of conclusions. CBIs show promise for improving self-compassion in some mothers. More research is needed to strengthen other conclusions. Integration of quantitative and qualitative data suggests interventions with evidence of qualitative themes (sharing experiences, self-acceptance, reflecting on difficulties and hope and trust for the future) may yield more significant and larger effects than those without. Chapter two is a qualitative research study using Constructivist Grounded Theory (CGT) methodology to investigate MHNSs’ understanding of compassion. Nine MHNSs were interviewed. Following CGT analysis, a theoretical model was constructed. Compassion was understood as an interrelated set of areas, namely “Pure concern for other”; Doing good, being good; Safe to learn; ‘”We’re all in this together” and Care for self for others leading to a core concept of ‘Connecting’. For MHNSs, compassion involves primarily connecting with their patients alongside connecting with values, their course and mentors, their cohort and tentatively with themselves. Chapter three is a first-person reflective account of the author’s research experience. The account is shaped by the three systems of emotion regulation from Gilbert (2009). Personal and systemic factors affecting the author’s threat, drive and soothe systems are discussed before concluding with a focus on the future.

title: Severity over source: Understanding transgressors' motive attributions of punishment
abstract: Punishment conveys social information to transgressors, who attribute motives to punishers. Drawing on the motive-attribution framework, we examined whether transgressors' attributions to competitive (i.e. harming transgressors), individualistic (i.e. managing one's own interests) and prosocial (i.e. healing relationships) motives differ depending on whether punishment is administered by victims (second-party punishment) or uninvolved observers (third-party punishment), and how these attributions relate to downstream affective, relational and behavioural outcomes. In an incentivized Stealing Game, participants could steal valuable points and were punished either by the victim or an observer. Subsequently, transgressors reported their motive attributions, affect and willingness to reconcile and completed a measure of prosocial behaviour towards an unrelated other. Contrary to predictions, motive attributions did not systematically differ between second- and third-party punishment, except that third-party punishment was more strongly attributed to reputational concerns (i.e. a subdimension of individualistic motive attribution). Punishment severity emerged as an important predictor, with harsher sanctions linked to stronger competitive and individualistic attributions. Competitive motive attribution, in turn, was associated with higher negative affect and lower positive affect, willingness to reconcile and prosocial behaviour. Overall, transgressors' responses to punishment were less clearly shaped by who punished and more closely linked to punishment severity and motive attribution.

title: The Role of the Effectiveness of Mosque Social Activities and Their Consistency in Repetition Donation Decisions (Case Study of Masjid Raya Al Insan)
abstract: Mosques play a vital role in Islam, serving not only as places of worship but also as centers for various social activities and economic empowerment, including the collection of social funds such as zakat, infaq, and sadaqah (charity). However, data from the 2024 Mosque Information System (SIMAS) of the Ministry of Religious Affairs of the Republic of Indonesia shows that of the total 694,725 mosques and prayer rooms, only 28,138 have a Mosque Welfare Agency (BKM), indicating that the majority of mosque management remains traditional and has not adopted modern management. Masjid Raya Al Insan (MRAI) in Kebayoran Lama, South Jakarta, is known for frequently holding social and humanitarian activities, both routine and incidental, for the congregation and the community living around the mosque. Previous research has examined factors such as transparency, accountability, the attitude of mosque management, and the social and religious influences of donors on trust and donation decisions. However, there is still little research that specifically examines the role of the effectiveness of mosque social activities and their consistency on repeat donation decisions. Using a qualitative case study method through in-depth interviews with administrators and donors, this study evaluates the role of the effectiveness and consistency of MRAI's social programs on repeat donations. The results show that the effectiveness of social activities is assessed by the emotional impact and tangible solutions for the community, not simply by statistical figures. It was found that repeat donation decisions are driven by a strong synergy between theological motivation and trust in the integrity of the administrators. Specifically, the consistency of social programs proved to be a key factor in building donor loyalty, validating the paradigm that "busy mosques" that actively distribute funds actually attract more donations. The study concluded that program consistency creates a sense of security and inner satisfaction for donors. As a recommendation, mosque administrators need to immediately undertake digital transformation in transparent financial reporting and implement Customer Relationship Management (CRM) to maintain donor relationships to ensure the sustainability of funding for community programs.

title: Random Forest for Multi-Output Analysis of University Students' Prosocial Behaviors
abstract: This study examines differential effects that different demographic variables and the subgroup-based community management model in universities on college students' prosocial behavior. Our dataset includes survey responses from 307 students enrolled in universities implementing this management model and 200 students from non-implementing universities. We employed the Random Forest algorithm to training AI model on 90% of the participant sample and reserving the remaining 10% for validation. The model achieved a prediction accuracy of 96.08%, demonstrating strong reliability in assessing the relationship between community-based subgroup management and prosocial behavioral outcomes. Furthermore, Random Forest shows the importance of independent variables.

title: How social norms emerge: the interindividual actor-critic
abstract: Social norms shape a vast range of human behaviors, from everyday interactions to major life choices. Yet, existing theories of norm emergence typically focus either on why certain norms arise (substantive properties) or on how they spread and persist (dynamical properties), often making conflicting assumptions. Here, we propose a unified account in which norms prescribing how one ought to act emerge naturally from the fundamental algorithms that guide learning—whether in social or non-social settings. Our account builds on recent advances in decision-making and emotion research that have highlighted ‘actor-critic’ models as a core mechanism of learning from feedback. We extend this mechanism to social settings by assuming that it is not only we who critique our actions, others critique our actions as well. By simulating this interindividual form of learning, we show that it uniquely produces group behavior that exhibits both substantive and dynamical properties of real-world social norms, including prosociality, ingroup bias, stickiness, S-shaped curves, and local conformity / global diversity. Our framework thus offers a uniquely parsimonious way to bridge the gap between individual learning and group behavior.

title: Evaluation of Co-Production in Adolescent Health Research: A Mixed Methods Study From Born in Bradford.
abstract: Co-production is often viewed as best practice for involving the public in research, while measures such as sharing power, reciprocity, and relationship-building are seen as key guiding principles. However, implementing co-production and its underlying principles remains challenging, with limited evaluative work examining how these principles are applied in practice, particularly within large-scale studies and with young people. This study aimed to explore whether Born in Bradford's (BiB) co-production values and principles have been embedded in BiB Age of Wonder (AoW), a longitudinal study following over 20,000 Bradford teenagers through secondary school and into early adulthood. This evaluation used a mixed-methods approach. Participants included parents, young people, teachers, and community members. Quantitative data was collected via an online survey (n = 79). Qualitative data was collected via four focus groups (n = 17). The survey and focus group topic guide were co-designed with young people, with questions designed to assess how well the principles and values of BiB's co-production strategy had been embedded in AoW. Descriptive statistics were used to explore the survey responses. Qualitative data was analysed using framework analysis. Survey and focus group findings indicated that co-production group members mostly agreed or strongly agreed that the nine principles of co-production had been embedded in AoW. However, 'sharing power' and 'community engagement' were found to be areas that could be improved, with participants calling for earlier involvement in research design, clearer feedback loops, and outreach beyond existing groups. We found evidence that the values and principles of co-production have been embedded in AoW co-production. Suggestions for improvement include shaping research agendas through earlier involvement, deeper engagement with schools and communities, and paid peer research posts. Future steps include (1) developing sustainable peer research strategies to deepen co-production, and (2) incorporating perspectives from diverse stakeholders including budget holders, facilitators, researchers and public contributors in future evaluations. Members of the public were involved in the study conceptualisation, methods development and implementation. The survey and focus group topic guide were co-designed with young people from BiB Age of Wonder co-production groups. Co-production group members were also involved as participants in the surveys and focus groups.

title: Comparing harmonization in medicines regulation and health technology assessment in Europe: lessons for the EU HTA regulation.
abstract: The European Union (EU) has long pursued harmonization in medicines regulation and, more recently, in health technology assessment (HTA). The European Medicines Agency (EMA) and the EU HTA Regulation (EU HTAR) represent key milestones in these respective trajectories. This study compares the harmonization trajectories of EU medicines regulation and EU HTA to identify lessons relevant for EU HTAR implementation. We used a multi-method qualitative approach combining a narrative literature review with online focus groups involving eighteen regulatory and policy experts. The review explored the historical development of harmonization in both policy areas. The focus-group analysis examined perspectives on collaboration, harmonization dynamics, and implementation. Both policy areas moved from national arrangements and voluntary cooperation toward more formal EU-level structures. Medicines regulation developed earlier and resulted in more centralized procedures and binding EU-wide authorization decisions. EU HTA retains greater national responsibility for value judgments, pricing, and reimbursement. The two areas also differ in the scope and standardization of assessments. In both trajectories, harmonization was shaped by trust, willingness to collaborate, capacity differences, and legal and procedural contexts. Participants emphasized the importance of stepwise implementation, work sharing, and sustained dialogue, while anticipating variation in national JCA uptake and impact. Experience from EU medicines regulation highlights the importance of building trust and adapting collaboration to differences in national maturity and priorities. Harmonization should develop gradually through learning and refinement across diverse legal and procedural contexts. These lessons may support EU HTAR implementation and further development.

title: From silence to sharing: A six-month prospective study on adult disclosure of childhood sexual abuse.
abstract: Disclosure of childhood sexual abuse (CSA) is often assumed to be beneficial. However, prospective research examining outcomes associated with disclosure remains scarce, limiting evidence-based guidance for adults considering disclosure. The primary aim was to examine changes in posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms following first-time disclosure of CSA to personal contacts and to test whether perceived supportiveness of confidants' responses moderated these changes. The secondary aim was to explore characteristics of CSA disclosure. Forty adults with a history of CSA who had not previously disclosed the abuse to personal contacts completed two assessments, at baseline and at follow-up six months later. Participants who disclosed their CSA to a personal contact during the follow-up period were classified as disclosers, whereas those who did not were classified as non-disclosers. During the follow-up period, 60% (n = 24) disclosed for the first time to personal contacts, after on average 31.5 years (SD = 16.2), most often to friends (47%). Disclosers showed a clinically relevant, greater reduction in PTSD symptoms than non-disclosers. Perceived supportiveness of confidants' responses was moderate to high but did not significantly moderate changes in PTSD symptoms. First-time disclosure of CSA in adulthood to personal contacts was associated with a clinically relevant reduction in PTSD symptoms. Nevertheless, individual differences in symptom change indicate that outcomes following disclosure vary. Guidance should therefore move beyond the question of whether to disclose and consider when, under what circumstances, and for whom disclosure may be beneficial.

title: Impact of Migraine and Its Management in 5 Gulf Countries: Results of a Social Media Platforms Listening Study.
abstract: Migraine is a common neurological disorder that affects a significant proportion of the global population but remains largely underdiagnosed and undertreated. This study analyzed discussions related to migraines in English and Arabic across Kuwait, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Oman, and Qatar. Social media listening may help to identify gaps in migraine management and guide the development of strategies to address them. This study aims to analyze discussions related to migraines in both English and Arabic across various social media platforms. By applying social analytics to the bilingual discourse on migraines in the Gulf region, a region that is often underrepresented, we seek to integrate clinical perspectives with regional digital conversations and identify potential gaps in awareness and care pathways. The study was conducted using a retrospective and descriptive approach to social analytics. The study analyzed discussions about migraines from over 100 million websites in English and Arabic across Kuwait, Bahrain, the UAE, Oman, and Qatar between January 1, 2018, and June 30, 2022. Vendor-implemented, rule-based processes, including keyword matching, language identification, and structured data extraction, were used to evaluate publicly available content in English and Arabic. Out of 53,000 mentions, 33,920 (64%) occurred on X (formerly Twitter), and men were 1.1 times more likely to discuss migraines than women. Among patient conversations, the impact of migraines on overall health was often discussed, including mentions of pregnancy 1060 (2%), vision problems 1325 (2.5%), and sleep disruption 1590 (3%). Medications like paracetamol, aspirin, ibuprofen, and triptans were frequently mentioned, alongside self-management treatments such as cannabidiol softgels, cupping, and aroma oils. Patients often used TikTok to share experiences and seek advice. Many patients actively sought to connect and engage with other migraine sufferers for support and to share experiences. Social media served as a valuable source of information for patients, with health care professionals (HCPs) actively sharing insights and resources through these platforms. The study finds that analysis of migraine discourse across the 5 Gulf countries reveals active engagement by patients and HCPs in migraine-related discussions on various social media platforms. However, many rely on self-management and alternative medicine instead of seeking professional medical help, which leads to improper management of symptoms. The findings should be regarded as compelling descriptive signals in discourse rather than predictive or inferential outcomes. Social media listening may help to identify possible gaps in management and suggest areas for improvement, but these findings need further validation.

title: Symbolic promotions: Conceptualization and empirical investigation
abstract: Abstract Symbolic promotions are an increasingly prevalent marketing practice globally, yet little is known about how or when they influence consumer behavior. We conceptualize symbolic promotions as a distinct type of sales promotion that creates value by reinforcing consumers' social identity through shared group membership rather than by providing economic incentives, such as reward-based promotions, or supporting distant others, such as cause-related marketing promotions (CMPs). We investigate the effectiveness of symbolic promotions and their underlying mechanisms using a multimethod approach. A nine-year longitudinal field study of daily sales for 22,084 books demonstrates that an existing symbolic promotion ("On August 12, I buy a Quebec book!") generates a substantial increase in sales, with stronger effects for lesser-known brands than for well-known brands. A follow-up experiment uncovers the unique mechanisms underlying these effects, showing that symbolic promotions stimulate curiosity and community rootedness, which in turn enhance multiple types of behavioral intentions, i.e., the likelihood of participating in the promotion, sharing it on social media, and future brand consideration. Together, these findings position symbolic promotions as a distinct, complementary addition to firms’ promotional portfolios, and demonstrate how firms can leverage shared identities to create value beyond traditional monetary incentives, with implications for various stakeholders.

title: INSTITUTIONS THAT SCORE VIRTUE: A General Theory, with China's Social Credit System as the Principal Case — What Aristotle, Confucius, Han Feizi, Kant, Holmström–Milgrom, Bénabou–Tirole, Sandel and Tirole's Digital Dystopia Already Hold, and What Remains
abstract: Abstract States, platforms, employers, schools, rating agencies and parents increasingly attach consequences to records of conduct that bears a virtue’s name: trustworthiness, civility, integrity, generosity, sustainability, good behaviour. This article asks a general question — can an institution score virtue without changing what it scores? — and answers it with a theory of virtue-scoring institutions, tested against the largest such institution ever built, China’s social credit system, and illustrated on platform reputation, environmental, social and governance (ESG) ratings, workplace values appraisals and children’s reward charts. The first part addresses the question on which every other result depends: whether a rewarded act of virtue is the same act under different incentives or a different act. The answer is stated as a claim about act-types rather than act-tokens, which makes it indifferent to the dispute between coarse- and fine-grained theories of action: the virtues’ act-types are reason-involving, and an act whose operative reason is the reward does not instantiate them under either theory. Priority for this type claim is conceded to Aristotle (Nicomachean Ethics II.4), to Kant’s distinction between acting from duty and in accordance with it, and to Sandel’s corruption argument. What remains to the programme is the rest. An operator (civic occupation) states four conditions under which a scoring institution produces counterfeits, with the load-bearing condition that it inspects a display distinct from the substance and can neither take nor independently measure the substance. From it follow a classification of scoring components into four kinds with opposite verdicts; the Honour Roll Theorem (counterfeits concentrate on the reward side of an institution, not the punitive side); Double Blindness (scores displace acts as evidence of character, for the scorer and between the scored); the Occasion Trap (sanctions remove the occasions on which reform could be shown); and the Control Theorem (every increase in an institution’s control over its members either inverts their acts or removes the occasions for them, and none increases their freedom, which, when taken, passes to no one). China’s system is decomposed component by component against the theory, including the 2026 Administrative Measures for Credit Repair, read in the original. Five tests are registered; four use public data, and one of those needs neither a coder nor participants. The empirical sections on China, platforms and ESG are speculative extensions into fields with their own evidential standards; no specialist in those fields has reviewed this article, and nothing else in the programme may depend on them. The article contains no measurement of any human being. Keywords: virtue scoring; social credit system; China; reputation systems; ESG ratings; honours and awards; act individuation; Aristotle; Confucius; Han Feizi; Legalism; Kant; motivation crowding; Holmström–Milgrom; Bénabou–Tirole; Sandel; Tirole; Digital Dystopia; Wintrobe; sourcehood; counterfeit virtue; Philosophy of Virtues Highlights · The question whether rewarded virtue is still virtue is a question about act-types, not act-tokens; on that reading the answer is no under every standard theory of action, and priority belongs to Aristotle, Kant and Sandel. · A scoring institution produces counterfeit virtue only where it inspects a display and can neither take nor independently measure the substance; four kinds of scoring component follow, with opposite verdicts. · Counterfeits concentrate on honours and rewards, not on penalties: the Honour Roll Theorem. · Scores displace acts as evidence of character, for the institution and between its members: Double Blindness. · No increase in an institution’s control over its members increases their freedom; freedom taken by a power is not transferred to it but destroyed. Relevance Institutions that score virtue are spreading faster than any theory of what they do. Most debate treats them either as surveillance, to be resisted, or as measurement, to be improved. If this article is right, neither frame is adequate: a better metric of a display does not reach the substance, and the most consequential failures lie not in punishment but in honour. The theory gives designers, regulators and critics a component-level test that is indifferent to who administers the score — a state, a firm, a platform or a family — and tells them which components can be kept as the least of the losses, which must be abandoned, and which must be renamed. If it is wrong, the programme’s central results on capture and forgery have no purchase on the fastest-growing class of institutions in the world, and that should be known before those results are used in public argument.

title: Do Large Language Models Walk Their Talk? Measuring the Gap Between Implicit Associations, Self-Report, and Behavioral Altruism
abstract: We investigate whether Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit altruistic tendencies, and critically, whether their implicit associations and self-reports predict actual altruistic behavior. Using a multi-method approach inspired by human social psychology, we tested 24 frontier LLMs across three paradigms: (1) an Implicit Association Test (IAT) measuring implicit altruism bias, (2) a forced binary choice task measuring behavioral altruism, and (3) a self-assessment scale measuring explicit altruism beliefs. Our key findings are: (1) All models show strong implicit pro-altruism bias (mean IAT = 0.87, p < .0001), confirming models "know" altruism is good. (2) Models behave more altruistically than chance (65.6% vs. 50%, p < .0001), but with substantial variation (48-85%). (3) Implicit associations do not predict behavior (r = .22, p = .29). (4) Most critically, models systematically overestimate their own altruism, claiming 77.5% altruism while acting at 65.6% (p < .0001, Cohen's d = 1.08). This "virtue signaling gap" affects 75% of models tested. Based on these findings, we recommend the Calibration Gap (the discrepancy between self-reported and behavioral values) as a standardized alignment metric. Well-calibrated models are more predictable and behaviorally consistent; only 12.5% of models achieve the ideal combination of high prosocial behavior and accurate self-knowledge.

title: Reproductive Labour, Commodification, and Gestational Surrogacy in Greece: A materialist feminist approach
abstract: This paper examines surrogacy in Greece through a materialist and Marxist feminist framework grounded in Social Reproduction Theory, situating gestation within the political economy of reproductive labour under capitalism. While Greek law constructs surrogacy as an altruistic, non-commercial, and consensual act, such framing obscures the economic, affective, psychological and corporeal labour that gestation entails. Through an analysis of the Greek legislative context and an original reading of Greek surrogacy case law, the paper demonstrates how the legal framework operates as an ideological and repressive apparatus that depoliticises reproductive work and erases the surrogate’s labour, privileging the reproductive aspirations of intended parents. Situating surrogacy within a continuum of reproductive work, we highlight how alienation, understood in the Marxist sense of estrangement from one’s labour and its product, is produced materially and psychologically through moralised ideals of care, sacrifice, agency, and femininity. Making reproductive labour visible is the precondition for contesting its conditions of extraction, and a labour-centred reconceptualisation of surrogacy that repositions surrogates as reproductive workers opens space for collective contestation.

title: Food Addiction Symptoms in Adults with Alcohol Use Disorder.
abstract: Food addiction (FA) has been proposed as a phenotype sharing features with substance use disorders. Despite increasing recognition of food addiction as a behavioral phenotype with features overlapping substance use disorders, little is known about its prevalence or clinical significance among individuals with alcohol use disorder (AUD). To examine the prevalence of FA and to evaluate demographic, psychological, and alcohol related correlates in individuals with AUD. This cross-sectional analysis included 743 adults with AUD who were either treatment-seeking (Tx) (n = 534) for AUD and were enrolled in an inpatient program at the National Institutes of Health Clinical Center or non-treatment-seeking (non-Tx) (n = 209). FA symptoms were assessed using the Yale Food Addiction Scale, with ≥2 symptoms categorized as FA in this report. Multivariable logistic regression models adjusted for age, education, and income were conducted separately within each cohort. Among 743 adults with AUD, 238 (32.1%) met criteria for FA symptoms, with similar prevalence among Tx (32.6%) and non-Tx (30.6%) participants despite marked differences in clinical characteristics. Across both cohorts, FA was independently associated with higher body mass index, greater psychological distress, and greater alcohol dependence severity. Childhood trauma and poorer sleep quality were additionally associated with FA among treatment-seeking participants, whereas alcohol-related measures differed according to treatment status. FA was common among adults with AUD and was associated with greater psychological, behavioral, and metabolic burden regardless of treatment-seeking status. These findings suggest that FA identifies a clinically meaningful subgroup of individuals with AUD who may benefit from more comprehensive assessment and integrated treatment approaches.

title: Patient safety and employee voice : the role of second victims in overcoming the hierarchical challenge
abstract: Healthcare organisations have struggled to improve safety. Over the last 20 years rates of patient harm have remained at around 10%, despite implementation of various improvement initiatives linked to the patient safety movement. This study identifies key conditions perpetuating this safety ‘implementation gap’: 1) a hierarchical challenge and 2) second victim phenomenon. Employee voice is adopted as a sensitising concept. The aim is to identify conditions which moderate the hierarchical challenge, encouraging the enactment of voice, leading to prevention of further medical errors. This PhD’s original contribution to knowledge is: second victims are key actors in attenuating hierarchical barriers through enactment of positively valenced practices. Adopting a practice-based approach identifying medical errors as break-downs in professional practice, three cases of serious medical error at a single NHS Trust are chosen for comparative analysis. Data collection includes over 100 hours of observations, 50 interviews, and review of 35 documents. Evidence for a climate of silence was found in each case stemming from: a hierarchical culture, blame culture, and futility of voice. Acquiescent or defensive silence contributed directly to each serious medical error. Second victims were found in each case, generally experiencing guilt, shame, anger, and compassion. The recovery trajectory of these second victims varied, with one ‘thriving’ while others ‘survived’ or ‘dropped out’. Positively valenced practice changes, which set the conditions for voice, were enacted by affectively charged individuals, either the second victim themselves, or through a process of emotional contagion, their colleagues. These conditions for voice included: setting expectations for voice, management engendering voice, closer adherence to policy and standard operating procedures, and a reinvigorated sentiment of care. These changes led to development of a voice climate encouraging the enactment of both defensive and prosocial voice. A safety incident model of voice for second victims was developed and transferability discussed.

title: Assessment of child self-regulation: A review of ecological and structured approaches
abstract: The extent to which developmental science has mapped associations between cognitive, academic and socio-emotional functioning; caregiver reports and non-participant observation of young children was examined. Initially, 88 studies comprising over 300 effects were identified. The relationships between outcome measures and research design was described. Findings show that recurrent associations between task performance, behavioral report and naturalistic observation appear in this literature. The most frequently occurring comparisons in school settings were those between children’s disruptive-aggressive behavior, on-task/off-task behavior, prosocial behavior, externalizing problems, prosocial skills and early math and language achievement. In home settings, those between children’s positive/negative affect, engagement, compliance, temperament, cognitive and motor development were most common. Despite conceptual overlap, limited access to correlational data and between-study heterogeneity hinders cross-sample comparisons.

title: Moderate cardiac vagal tone predicts more cooperation in highly sensitive individuals
abstract: Cooperation, as a mutual collaboration, is a defining feature of human social life. Individual characteristics can influence cooperation. Recent studies have shown a quadratic relationship between cardiac vagal tone (CVT), an index of self-regulation, and prosocial behaviors. Individual differences in cooperation might also vary as a function of people's environmental sensitivity (ES), i.e., may be influenced by individual differences in the perception and processing of inner and external stimuli. We tested the direct and interactive effect of CVT and ES on cooperative behaviors in two independent samples. We measured heart rate and engagement in cooperative acts in 80 young adults (M = 23.61; SD = 1.60) who were also asked to self-report on ES. We found an inverted-U relationship between CVT and cooperative behaviors. ES, on the other hand, did not predict differences in cooperative behaviors but moderated the relationships between CVT and cooperation, although the magnitude of this result was small. Specifically, only among individuals with higher ES cooperative behaviors change as a function of CVT. Highly sensitive individuals with lower or higher CVT, were less cooperative than low sensitive ones. Subsequently, we replicated the same study design in a second sample of 88 undergraduate students (M = 23.69; SD = 4.91). Once again, we found evidence supporting the presence of an inverted-U relationship between CVT and cooperative behaviors, and we also found that ES moderated the relationships between the quadratic CVT term and cooperation.

title: Cooperation, Cognition, and the Elusive Role of Joint Agency
abstract: Abstract We propose an approach to the evolution of joint agency and cooperative behavior that contrasts with views that take joint agency to be a uniquely human trait. We argue that there is huge variation in cooperative behavior and that while much human cooperative behavior may be explained by invoking cognitively rich capacities, there is cooperative behavior that does not require such explanation. On both comparative and theoretical grounds, complex cognition is not necessary for forms of joint action or the evolution of cooperation. As a result, promising evolutionary approaches to cooperative behavior should explain how it arises across many contexts.

title: Sessizliğin Psikolojisi: Gazze Soykırımı Özelinde Küresel Seyirci (Bystander) Davranışının Sosyal-Din Psikolojik Analizi
abstract: Kitlesel şiddet olaylarının yalnızca failler tarafından değil, aynı zamanda bu olaylar karşısında sessiz kalan ve eyleme geçmeyen geniş kitleler tarafından da sürdürüldüğü kabul edilmektedir. Sosyal psikoloji literatüründe bu durum seyirci (bystander) davranışı kavramı çerçevesinde ele alınmış ve çoğunlukla yüz yüze acil durumlar bağlamında incelenmiştir. Ancak günümüzde insani krizler giderek daha fazla dijital medya aracılığıyla deneyimlenmekte, bireyler şiddet ve acıya doğrudan değil, sosyal medya ve çevrim içi haber platformları üzerinden tanıklık etmektedir. Bu nedenle mevcut kuramsal yaklaşımlar, coğrafi olarak uzak ve dijital olarak dolayımlanmış kitlesel şiddet bağlamlarında ortaya çıkan eylemsizliği açıklamada yetersiz kalmaktadır. Bu çalışma, 7 Ekim 2023’ten itibaren Gazze’de devam eden kitlesel şiddet karşısında gözlenen küresel dijital seyirci davranışını açıklamaya yönelik kuramsal bir model önermektedir. Çalışmanın temel amacı, aynı dini kimliğe sahip olan bireylerden bir kısmı soykırıma uğrarken diğer bireylerin bu soykırıma neden seyirci davranışı olarak pasif kaldığını sosyal psikolojik olarak açıklamaktır. Din psikolojisi literatürü, dindarlığın empati, prososyal davranış ve ahlaki duyarlılıkla ilişkili olduğunu göstermesine rağmen, bu eğilimlerin her zaman eyleme dönüşmediği görülmektedir. Çalışma, bu paradoksu açıklamayı amaçlamaktadır. Makalede sosyal psikoloji, din psikolojisi ve kitlesel şiddet literatürü bütünleştirilerek beş katmanlı bir psikososyal model geliştirilmiştir. İlk katman olan yapısal katman, dijital uyaran fazlalığı, zaman baskısı ve bilişsel daralma süreçlerinin bireylerin ahlaki dikkatini sınırladığını ileri sürmektedir. İkinci katman olan bilişsel katman, sorumluluğun uluslararası kuruluşlar, devletler ve diğer güçlü aktörlere devredilmesini açıklamaktadır. Üçüncü katman olan sosyal-normatif katman, Sessizlik Sarmalı Kuramı ve çoğulcu cehalet kavramları aracılığıyla, bireylerin çevrelerindeki sessizliği toplumsal bir norm olarak algılamalarını ve bu nedenle görüşlerini ifade etmekten kaçınmalarını açıklamaktadır. Dördüncü katman olan ahlaki meşrulaştırma katmanı, adil dünya inancı, ahlaki çözülme ve insandışılaştırma mekanizmalarının eylemsizliği nasıl meşrulaştırdığını ortaya koymaktadır. Son katman olan duygusal katman ise merhamet yorgunluğu, duygusal küntleşme ve psişik uyuşma süreçlerinin bireylerin empatik tepkilerini nasıl zayıflattığını açıklamaktadır. Model, bu katmanların birbirinden bağımsız değil, geri-beslemeli bir döngü içerisinde işlediğini ileri sürmektedir. Yapısal baskılar bilişsel uzaklaşmayı, bilişsel süreçler normatif sessizliği, normatif sessizlik ahlaki meşrulaştırmayı, ahlaki meşrulaştırma ise duygusal tükenmeyi beslemektedir. Duygusal tükenme de bireyin dikkat ve duyarlılığını daha da azaltarak döngüyü yeniden üretmektedir. Çalışmanın din psikolojisine özgün katkısı, dinî kimliği yardım davranışını doğrudan belirleyen bir değişken olarak değil, tüm modelin işleyişini etkileyen bütünleşik bir moderatör olarak kavramsallaştırmasıdır. Dinî kimlik, belirli koşullar altında seyirci davranışını azaltabileceği gibi, bazı durumlarda bu davranışı derinleştirebilmektedir. Gazze bağlamında geliştirilen bu model, aynı zamanda dijital çağda ortaya çıkan diğer kitlesel şiddet ve soykırım örneklerinde gözlenen ahlaki eylemsizliği anlamak için de kullanılabilecek genel bir kuramsal çerçeve sunmaktadır.

title: Oxytocin restores context-specific hyperaltruistic preference
abstract: Recent advances in moral decision-making research show people are hyperaltruistic by being more willing to sacrifice monetary gains to spare others from suffering than to spare themselves. Yet other studies indicate an opposite egoistic bias: subjects are less willing to harm themselves for others' benefits than for their own. These results underscore the complexities of moral decisions and demand a mechanistic explanation for hyperaltruistic preferences. We investigated hyperaltruism using trade-off choices combining monetary gains and painful electric shocks and choices combining monetary losses and shocks. Study 1 revealed that switching the decision context from gains to losses effectively eliminated the hyperaltruistic preference, accompanied by the altered relationship between subjects' instrumental harm (IH) trait attitudes and relative pain sensitivities. In the pre-registered study 2, we found that oxytocin, a neuropeptide linked to parochial altruism, restored the context-dependent hyperaltruistic preference. Furthermore, oxytocin increased the degree to which subjects framed the task as harming others, which mediated the correlation between IH and relative pain sensitivities. Thus, the loss decision context and oxytocin diminished and restored the mediation effect of subjective harm framing, respectively. Our results help elucidate the psychological processes underpinning the contextual specificity of hyperaltruism and carry implications in promoting prosocial interactions.

title: 'Can I tell you about the funny bit?': Working alongside children as citizen scientists to explore shared Reading practices in the home.
abstract: Shared reading research has traditionally focused on developmental outcomes yet rarely positions children as co-constructors of knowledge about their own literacy practices. Grounded in a child-rights informed and ecological developmental framework, this study positions children as citizen scientists to examine how shared reading is experienced within the relational context of home life. Using a participatory action research approach, 109 children aged 7-11 participated in 21 CoNavigator sessions. CoNavigator is a tactile, dialogic methodology that embeds participants directly in both data generation and primary analysis. In peer-led groups, children collaboratively constructed three-dimensional conceptual maps in response to the prompt 'shared reading at home', collectively defining what shared reading is, what it ought to be and what should change to support it. Children generated, organized, negotiated and interpreted their own data in real time, functioning as analytic collaborators rather than research subjects. While recognizing shared reading as developmentally valuable, children emphasized autonomy, emotional safety and attentive co-presence as central to sustained engagement. They reconceptualized 'sharing' to include post-reading dialogue and relational proximity rather than solely simultaneous co-reading. Experiences framed as overly corrective or compulsory were associated with disengagement, and the findings challenge outcome-driven models of home literacy support.

title: Dialogic communication and audience engagement in Hispanic health marketing on X: A computational analysis.
abstract: This study investigated the overarching themes and dialogic features of the three national-level Hispanic health organizations (i.e., NHMA, NAHH, NHHF). The focus is on how these health organizations utilize social media for Hispanic health and how the themes and dialogic features are associated with public engagement on social media. To achieve this, the study employed structural topic modeling on 18,430 X posts from 2018 to 2023 and negative binomial regression to predict user amplification engagement (e.g., liking, sharing). The study identified four broad thematic areas: health equity and advocacy, health education and disease prevention, professional and organizational development, and research and community engagement. Negative binomial regression analyses showed that amplification engagement was associated with both communicative features and thematic contexts. Hyperlinks were negatively associated with likes and shares, while multiple interaction effects indicated that the associations between dialogic features and engagement varied across thematic contexts. These findings suggest that the effectiveness of X-based communication features depends on message topic rather than operating uniformly across health communication contexts. The study contributes to health marketing research by demonstrating how computational methods can identify the thematic and affordance-based conditions under which organizational health messages are more likely to generate public amplification in digital environments.

title: Mothers' Experiences From Prenatal Diagnosis to Home Following Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia: A Qualitative Study.
abstract: To explore the experiences of mothers who completed the care pathway following a diagnosis of congenital diaphragmatic hernia and identify implications for nursing and midwifery practice. A qualitative descriptive phenomenological study. Semi-structured interviews were conducted in February 2023 with 21 mothers who had completed the congenital diaphragmatic hernia care pathway between 2019 and 2022 at an academic referral hospital for fetal surgery in Northern Italy. Women whose pregnancy was not carried to term, those who experienced fetal or neonatal loss, and those receiving ongoing psychological support were not included. Data were analysed thematically using a descriptive phenomenological approach. Five themes were identified across diagnosis, decision-making, specialised care, childbirth, and the postnatal transition home. Mothers experienced the pathway as interconnected transitions characterised by uncertainty, repeated adaptation, and changes in the maternal role. Specialist counselling improved clarity but did not eliminate prognostic uncertainty. Midwives emerged as central relational figures during childbirth, while mothers highlighted communication, parental involvement, continuity, and preparation for discharge. Among mothers represented in this study, informational, emotional, relational, and practical needs evolved from prenatal diagnosis to home care but remained closely interconnected. Nursing and midwifery priorities may include reinforcing complex information, preparing women for childbirth and possible neonatal separation, facilitating parental involvement, and supporting readiness for home care. The study addresses limited understanding of how maternal needs evolve across the congenital diaphragmatic hernia care continuum. Uncertainty, adaptation, and changes in the maternal role persisted across successive transitions. Findings may inform nursing, midwifery, and multidisciplinary support across fetal, maternity, neonatal, and community care. The COREQ checklist guided reporting. Mothers contributed as study participants by sharing their experiences; they were not involved in study design, analysis, or manuscript preparation.

title: How Can We Reach You? An Overview of Establishing Effective Recruitment Strategies for Young Women Breast Cancer Survivors.
abstract: Young women (aged 18-50) breast cancer survivors often face troubling sexual side effects resulting from cancer and cancer treatment. Research interventions can target young women's unique needs, but recruitment for this population remains a challenge. We sought to determine an effective strategy to recruit young women breast cancer survivors for our remote, nurse-led sexual health psychoeducational intervention EMBRACE (Empowerment through Mind and Body Reclamation After Cancer Experience). Our 5 major recruitment methods were: (1) using a study website; (2) distributing a digital study flyer; (3) placing physical rack cards in 2 nearby states; (4) employing snowball sampling through word-of-mouth; and (5) sharing Facebook posts. Sixty-four young women breast cancer survivors expressed interest in being screened. They learned about our study through Facebook groups (n = 24; 38%), Facebook pages (n = 17; 27%), word-of-mouth (n = 16; 25%), Google searches (n = 4; 6%), and undisclosed searches (n = 3; 4%). Of the 64 women we screened, 55 met eligibility criteria, and 53 provided consent (96.4%). We withdrew 4 women who did not meet eligibility criteria, resulting in a sample of 49 women. Sharing directly with established cancer survivorship Facebook groups was the most effective recruitment strategy. Leveraging relationships using social media is the best method for recruiting young women breast cancer survivors. We recommend initiating contact with Facebook groups early in the development of the study. Collaborating with partners on social media was the most effective recruitment method.

title: a matter of perspective
abstract: Perspective-taking, the mental act of simulating an ‘other’s’ situation, is widely recognised as being fundamental to the proper functioning of critical thinking and belief-formation and in promoting empathy, social and cultural competence, and prosocial outcomes. Increasingly featured in learning continua in and across disciplines, and whose elicitation and development features strongly in Philosophy for/with Children (P4wC) and other Community of Philosophical Inquiry (CoPI) styled programs, it is commonly treated as a unitary concept. As an initial teacher educator on dialogic pedagogies, and experienced facilitator trainer in P4wC, here I argue against a unidimensional conception of perspective-taking in favour of a multidimensional one. Six perspective-taking types are proposed, defined by their frames of reference, or ‘deictic fields,’ what I call Somatic, Agentive, Sociative, Temporal, Spatial, and Alethic. Using a conceptual analysis approach and leaning on the cognate fields of psychology and moral philosophy, I argue that different perspective-taking types implicate different categories of decentric thinking requiring the application of different kinds of cognitive proficiencies and dexterities. I argue, further, that different perspective-taking types, and combination of types, bring with them different sorts of affordances for the thinking subject, as well as precipitating some familiar, and some not so familiar, challenges and deterrents. A better understanding of perspective-taking types, I conclude, could be used to assist P4wC/CoPI practitioners in better cultivating this competency and ought to inform empirical assessments into the impact that such programs might have on children’s decentric thinking.

title: Cultural Models of Everyday Love in Contemporary Spain: A Mixed‐Methods Cultural Consensus Study
abstract: ABSTRACT Using a sequential mixed‐method approach guided by Cultural Consensus Theory, we examined shared agreement about daily experiences that evoke feelings of love in the Spanish culture. In Study 1, we conducted semi‐structured interviews ( n = 54), two‐person interviews ( n = 6) and focus groups (3–5 participants; n = 40). Qualitative analyses found recurring experiences centred on explicit affection, dependable support and care, quality time and thoughtful actions. In Study 2, a representative sample of Spaniards ( N = 502) evaluated these experiences to assess if cultural agreement elicit feelings of love. Cognitive psychometric analysis revealed strong shared agreement. Experiences most likely to evoke love involved support and dependability, shared quality time and explicit expressions of love, particularly within close relationships such as family, partners and friends. In contrast, controlling or possessive behaviours from romantic or familial ties were unlikely to elicit love. These findings advance social psychological theory by demonstrating that everyday love can be understood as a form of shared cultural knowledge, specifically a relational social schema that can be empirically identified through Cultural Consensus Theory.
